issues.legal_issue: The transport authority may be empowered to alter the starting places and termini of public service vehicles by a rule made to control transport vehicles.
material_facts: The governing rule was amended to allow the transport authority, after notice to affected parties and for good and proper reasons, to fix or alter starting places and termini.
The authority used the amended rule to move the starting place and terminus from an existing bus-stand to another stand for the convenience of the travelling public.
The governing law authorized rules for controlling transport vehicles and allowed restrictions on picking up or setting down passengers at specified places.
issues.conclusion: The rule was within the rule-making power and the authority could use it to alter the starting places and termini.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 68(1), 68(2)(r) and 68(2)(za) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, the power to make rules for controlling transport vehicles includes the power to regulate and alter bus-stands; prohibiting passenger pick-up or set-down at specified places can result in a stand ceasing to serve that purpose. A duly notified stand is one notified by the Transport Authority, not necessarily by a municipality. Sections 270(b), 270(c) and 270(e) of the Madras District Municipalities Act do not displace the Transport Authority's traffic-control powers. Rules made under statutory rule-making authority are part of the statute and are not on the same footing as by-laws considered against general law; the Court also distinguished the discussion of by-laws in Craies on Statute Law.

rule.if: challenge_to_transport_stand_order and law_authorized_transport_control_rules and law_allowed_place_specific_passenger_restrictions and authority_altered_vehicle_stands

predicates.challenge_to_transport_stand_order: A proceeding challenges an order altering where public service vehicles may start or terminate journeys.
predicates.law_authorized_transport_control_rules: The governing law authorized the executive to make rules for controlling transport vehicles.
predicates.law_allowed_place_specific_passenger_res: The governing law allowed rules restricting passenger pick-up or set-down at specified places.
predicates.authority_altered_vehicle_stands: The transport authority changed the places used as starting points or termini for public service vehicles.

issues.definition: When a challenge to a transport-stand order concerns an alteration made under a regime authorizing transport-control rules and place-specific passenger restrictions, the rule means that the stand-alteration rule is within the authority's rule-making power.

issues.legal_issue: Restricting the use of a bus-stand for passenger pick-up and set-down on outward journeys does not unreasonably restrict the right to carry on business when the business is not prohibited and the restriction serves public convenience.
material_facts: The bus-stand owner was prevented from using the site to pick up or set down passengers travelling on outward journeys.
The owner was not prohibited from carrying on the bus-stand business altogether, and the stand could still be used for carrying passengers into the town and vice versa.
The authority changed the starting and terminal points for the convenience of the travelling public.
The change reduced the income the owner had received from the stand's use for outward journeys.
issues.conclusion: The restriction was reasonable and did not infringe the constitutional right to carry on business.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) protects the right to carry on a profession, occupation, trade or business, but there is no fundamental right to conduct business wherever one chooses. Under Article 19, a restriction imposed by an executive authority in the interest of public convenience is not unreasonable merely because it reduces income or eliminates a particular use of the business premises, where the authority has power to impose it. Sections 47(1)(a) and 48(v) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, reflect the relevance of public interest and specified passenger pick-up and set-down points in regulating transport.

rule.if: challenge_to_business_restriction and business_not_prohibited_entirely and restriction_limited_to_outward_passenger_use and authority_acting_for_public_convenience

predicates.challenge_to_business_restriction: A proceeding challenges a restriction affecting the use of premises in connection with a business.
predicates.business_not_prohibited_entirely: The business operator remained able to carry on the business in some form.
predicates.restriction_limited_to_outward_passenger: The restriction barred passenger pick-up or set-down for outward journeys but did not bar every use of the premises for passenger transport.
predicates.authority_acting_for_public_convenience: The authority imposed the restriction for the convenience of the travelling public.

issues.definition: Where a business remains possible, the restriction is limited to outward passenger use, and the authority acts for public convenience, the rule means that the restriction is reasonable.

issues.legal_issue: An order altering transport-vehicle stands is not invalid for want of consultation or impartiality when the affected operator receives notice and an opportunity to respond, the authority consults a suitable public body, and allegations of bad faith or bias are unsupported.
material_facts: The transport authority gave the bus-stand owner notice of the proposed change, received the owner's written objections, and heard the owner and the municipality.
The authority consulted the municipality before making the order.
The owner alleged that the municipality was acting to displace him, but the Court found no material supporting bad faith.

The District Collector who presided over the authority's meeting had opened the replacement municipal stand, but he acted in an executive capacity rather than in a judicial or quasi-judicial capacity.
issues.conclusion: The consultation and decision-making process did not invalidate the order; the claims of bad faith and bias were rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 268 required notice to affected parties and permitted consultation with another authority as the Transport Authority considered desirable; consultation was discretionary, and consultation with the municipality was within the authority's powers. The Court found no evidentiary basis for bad faith and held that the Collector's executive conduct did not attract the scrutiny applicable to a judicial or quasi-judicial decision-maker.

rule.if: challenge_to_transport_stand_order and affected_operator_received_notice_and_hearing and local_authority_was_consulted and consultation_was_discretionary and bad_faith_evidence_absent and decision_maker_acted_executively

predicates.challenge_to_transport_stand_order: A proceeding challenges an order altering where public service vehicles may start or terminate journeys.
predicates.affected_operator_received_notice_and_he: The operator affected by the proposed change received notice, submitted objections, and was heard.
predicates.local_authority_was_consulted: The transport authority consulted a local public authority before making the change.
predicates.consultation_was_discretionary: The governing rule left the choice of whether to consult another authority to the transport authority.
predicates.bad_faith_evidence_absent: The person challenging the order did not provide material supporting the allegation of bad faith.
predicates.decision_maker_acted_executively: The decision-maker performed the relevant function in an executive rather than judicial or quasi-judicial capacity.

issues.definition: In a challenge to a transport-stand order, when the affected operator is heard, a suitable public authority is consulted where consultation is discretionary, and claims of bad faith or bias lack supporting facts, the rule means that the order is not invalid for process or bias.
